title: Salmon: protein, omega-3, fat, and calories

seo.title: Salmon nutrition: protein, omega-3, fat, and calories
seo.meta_description: Salmon commonly provides about 18–22 g protein and 180–210 calories per 100 g depending on species and origin. A serving can provide around 2 g EPA+DHA.
seo.search_intent: Understand salmon nutrition and why species, wild versus farmed origin, raw versus cooked state, and smoked preparation change the numbers.

excerpt: Salmon combines roughly 18–22 g protein per 100 g with considerably more fat than lean white fish. That fat raises calories, but it is also where salmon carries substantial EPA and DHA.
content_html:
“Salmon is a fatty fish rich in omega-3” is accurate but incomplete. Salmon does not have one fixed nutrition profile. Species, feed, wild versus farmed origin, and cooking all shift protein, fat, calories, and EPA+DHA.

A practical range per 100 g

NutrientRepresentative fresh/cooked salmon range
Calories~180–210 kcal
Protein~18–22 g
Fat~10–13 g
Carbohydrate0 g
EPA + DHAoften ~1.8–2.2 g/100 g for Atlantic salmon references

Using a range is more accurate than pretending every salmon fillet is identical.

A normal serving provides a substantial protein dose

At 20 g protein per 100 g, a 5-ounce serving provides roughly 28 g protein. At 22 g per 100 g, the same serving is about 31 g.

If a 100 g raw portion loses 20 g water during cooking, the nutrients are now concentrated in about 80 g of cooked fish. That is why cooked salmon can show a higher protein value per 100 g without creating protein.

Salmon is much fattier than lean white fish

A salmon fillet with 12 g fat per 100 g may contain roughly 10 g more fat than a very lean fish with 1–2 g. That difference alone accounts for about 90 calories.

But some of that fat is EPA and DHA. NIH lists about 0.59 g EPA plus 1.24 g DHA in a 3-ounce serving of cooked farmed Atlantic salmon, for 1.83 g combined.

Farmed and wild salmon are not nutritionally identical

NIH notes that omega-3 content varies widely among fish and that farmed fish can contain high EPA and DHA levels depending on feed composition. It is therefore inaccurate to assume wild salmon always contains more omega-3.

Fresh and smoked salmon answer different nutrition questions

Smoking and curing can leave protein near the same broad 18–25 g/100 g range while sodium rises from roughly 100 mg/100 g in fresh references to well over 1,000 mg/100 g in many smoked products.

That is why a “salmon” comparison should state whether the product is fresh, canned, or smoked.

The useful takeaway

Salmon commonly provides about 10–13 g fat and 180–210 calories/100 g, versus roughly 1–2 g fat and 65–100 calories in many lean white fish. That additional fat also carries EPA and DHA, so species and preparation matter when interpreting the numbers.

faq.question: How much protein is in salmon?
faq.answer: Depending on species and preparation, roughly 18–22 g per 100 g. A 5-ounce serving commonly provides around 26–31 g.

faq.question: How much omega-3 is in salmon?
faq.answer: It varies. NIH lists about 1.83 g EPA+DHA in a 3-ounce serving of cooked farmed Atlantic salmon.

faq.question: Is smoked salmon nutritionally the same as fresh salmon?
faq.answer: No. Protein and fat can be similar, but smoked salmon can contain much more sodium because of curing.
